newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Bank of England ups interest rate to 6.5 pct.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Bank of England ups interest rate to 6.5 pct.

text.p: The Bank of England's new monetary policy committee, put in charge of interest rates by the Labour government, raised official rates to 6.5 percent from 6.25 percent after its first meeting on Friday.
It was the first time since the central bank was nationalised in 1945 that it had changed interest rates without being instructed by the government.

The decision was consistent with the bank's argument in recent months that rampant consumer spending in Britain carried the risk of a resurgence in inflation if it was not checked by higher interest rates.
The pound gained half a pfennig to above 2.82 marks after the news, while share prices were little changed.
The Halifax, Britain's largest mortgage lender, immediately raised the cost of home loans by 0.35 percentage points to 7.95 percent.

In its statement, the bank said recent economic data had not changed the view it took in its inflation report last month that "on present evidence, there is still likely to be a need for some further moderate tightening of policy in the months ahead.
"The committee accordingly voted to raise the bank's repo rate by 0.25 percent to 6.50 percent," it said.

"It believes that this action to tighten the monetary stance, taken with the aim of meeting the government's inflation target, offers the best chance of achieving continued growth in output and employment at a sustainable pace."

Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Gordon Brown astounded financial markets within days of taking office last month by ceding the right to set interest rates to the bank, saying he wanted to free monetary policy from short-term political considerations.

Markets welcomed Brown's move as evidence of Labour's commitment to prudent economic policies but former Conservative Prime Minister John Major said it was folly to relinquish one of the main levers of economic power.
Brown also raised rates to 6.25 percent from 6.0 percent on May 6 in his first and last such decision.

Because the last increase was only a month ago, some economists had speculated that the bank might hold off to see if Labour's first budget on July 2 would raise the tax burden to dampen consumer demand.

The monetary policy committee is chaired by Bank of England Governor Eddie George, an inflation hawk, and also comprises deputy governor Howard Davies and the central bank's executive directors Mervyn King and Ian Plenderleith.
Two newly appointed outside members, Professors Charles Goodhart and Willem Buiter, had votes at the two-day meeting.
Sir Alan Budd, chief economic adviser to the Treasury, was present as a non-voting observer, while DeAnne Julius, British Airways Plc chief economist, will join the committee in September.
Full minutes of the inaugural meeting will be published in six weeks' time.
But the bank has previously acknowledged that policy-makers face a dilemma over monetary policy.

Higher interest rates mean the pound, which has already gained nearly 20 percent in value against major currencies since last summer, could appreciate further, making life even tougher for British exporters.
However, the services sector, which accounts for two-thirds of gross domestic product (GDP), is booming.

This, coupled with the fact that millions of Britons will receive "windfalls" totalling around 30 billion pounds ($48.8 billion) as mutually owned building societies and insurance companies turn themselves into banks, appears to have swayed the monetary committee.
Jeremy Peat, chief economist at the Royal Bank of Scotland, welcomed the move.
"The new monetary policy committee is to be commended for its first decision," he said.

"The strength of demand is likely to persist, bringing significant risks for inflation in 18 months' time. We are pleased to see the Bank of England using its new powers in such a forthright way." ($ = 0.615 British Pounds)
